review:
Yesterday you could get everything in-game by playing the game, today they removed that feature and now if you want everything in game you have to pay real money for it.

They essentially removed the entire endgame gameplay loop and put the rewards you could previously earn from gameplay into the cash shop instead.

Yesterday I was planning to buy more Ubisoft games. Today I am not.

Ubisoft released a "big update" which was just them taking pre-existing content and putting it behind a paywall.

You now have to pirate the game to play it in its original form.

Actual scammers, Steam should delist every Ubisoft game for this kind of behavior.

Wildlands has been one of my favourite games for years, and it's been great to see it be given some much needed love for the 25th Anniversary. The free update, QOL features, Last Rites mission, re-licensing the Predator mission, and anniversary gifts are awesome- and I can fully understand a few bugs coming along with poking about a nearly decade old game.

But Ubisoft's keen-as-ever buisness acumen on this is borderline insane.

Good news is a bunch of the premium store stuff has been rebundled at lower costs, or made free entirely.

Bad news is you can no longer earn the blue premium store credits to buy any of it because Daily/Weekly challenges have seemingly been entirely removed, as have all three types of loot crates.

Meaning no more blue credits from duplicate drops. This also means any prestige credits you can still earn (through say Tier 1 mode) can go towards little to nothing (boosters, supply points, skill points). Even if I bought what I could it looks like I'll permanantly be stuck with 75 of them because nothing in the store deals in denominations of less than a hundred. In addition it looks like any previously crate related item that remains locked is now fully paywalled in the store and can now only be bought via Microtransaction purchased credits. Taking previously earnable content in a beloved game and paywalling after this long it is dastardly work Ubisoft.

This also kills the classic promise of "You can earn most of the content in the game through play." as the one way to very slowly earn that premium content as I've been doing by coming back to GR Wildlands near daily for months on end in order to buy one or two of the weapon packs that interested me- is now removed from the game.

This is also the one thing that had kept me coming back regularly to play. The daily challenges were easily replayable and mostly entertaining remixes on completed missions with unique constraints- and community goals were endearing to see chipped away. I really hope their removal was in error, because it’d be so entertaining to see the predator mission looped into dailies- and most of the store issues I mentioned could be fixed by simply either having a small amount of blue credits be rewarded instead of crates, or orange credits rewarded with some small low ratio option to “buy” blue credits with them.

As of now, besides polishing off the new missions and the last of Fallen Ghosts- I don't know what's left to keep me coming back to a game I love playing with the thinnest excuse.

In my region it is currently: Cheaper to buy the On-Sale full package Definitive Edition of the game I already own the prior Ultimate Edition of- than it is to buy the Definitive Edition Upgrade which is currently more expensive than the full price of the base game- in order to access 1 DLC from launch that should have been included in the Ultimate Edition already, and 2 cosmetic DLC packs. Not including the Predator DLC: purchasable separately from your online game store of choice- or in game for credits you can't earn anymore and thus also being from your online game store of choice but with extra steps. Why is the Definitive Edition on sale at launch but the Definitive Edition Upgrade isn’t? Why do neither use steam’s bundle system- or scale their cost by how many of the DLCs so many long time players already own? I have a migraine.

I get the 'good' that comes from this update, but the poorly thought out 'bad' outweighs it shamefully.

I really hope this review becomes quickly outdated, because the game itself otherwise is phenomenal. I just can’t recommend it in this state.

[h1][b]Introduction[/b][/h1]
The last time I played the first installment of the Ghost Recon series was over a decade ago, so coming back to its successor felt naturally exciting. The differences between Wildlands and the original are vast. Thanks to that, I enjoy exploring the game more than I could ever hope for. This review will surely give you heaps of insight into the game, without a single spoiler.

[h2]Summary[/h2]
Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon® Wildlands (GRW) is a PvE-focused military tactical FPS, where you assume the role of special forces operators, known as Ghosts, in a reactive and immense recreation of Bolivia to take down the savage drug organization known as the Santa Blanca Cartel.

[table]
[tr]
	[th]😇Wins[/th]
	[th]💀Sins[/th]
[/tr]
[tr]
	[td]- Massive playable areas.
- Diverse, detailed, and beautiful ecosystems with realistic weather conditions and day/night cycle.
- Lifelike NPCs with schedules and practical actions.
- Fully customizable Ghosts Squad.
- Military role-playing.
- Well-assorted weaponry and satisfying gunplay.
- Sandbox gameplay.
- Limitless replay value.
- Playable without internet connection.
- Accessible to casual, hardcore, and immersion-oriented players.
- Seamless (for the most part) and unrestricted co-op experience. [/td]
	[td]- Unmemorable, no-stakes story.
- Repetitive and predictable mission objectives.
- Inactive PvP.
- Seldomly unresponsive AI teammates.
- The lack of tactical elements like camouflage, corpses interaction, disguise.[/td]
[/tr]
[/table]

[h1][b]In-depth Analysis[/b][/h1]
[h2]How Open World Should Be[/h2]
GRW features 21 provinces inside eleven highly detailed and realistic ecosystems, making each visit to these areas feel like a whole new experience. From shallow swamps, open green lands, elevated forest valleys, lakes, waterfalls to snowy mountains. With the character creation available at any time, you can customize your whole squad - composed of Nomad (your playable Ghost leader), Midas, Holt, and Weaver (your AI teammates) - to alternate their appearances and fade into nature’s background. While most locations and the geography of the world are purely fictitious, a few recreated landscapes are based on their real-life counterparts, like the terrifyingly accurate Death Road, or the beautiful shallow salt lake Red Lagoon, and many more for you to explore. 

Although made up, all other locations still feel believable enough to be indistinguishable from real life, with NPC civilians all having proper interactions with each other and the environments, like celebrating in costumes, playing football, or simply swiping the floor. Watching them react is fun and intriguing, which is something I rarely enjoy in any other games. Sincerely, I think this fictional version of Bolivia has become my new standard of how an open-world game should be. 
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2702247587
[h2]Choose How to Operate[/h2]
Since the world is reactive with weather conditions, day/night cycle, along with enemies and civilians acting accordingly to their set daily routines, you too can choose how to handle them and use the environments to your advantage. Almost all cartel thugs, even the Unidad - dirty government soldiers - sleep and eat at night (except during special operations), making them vulnerable to a stealthy operator. During nights, enemies are harder to see, and so are you. It'd be wise to scout out the whole area using a binocular or a drone. With night-vision goggles equipped, you'll be the unseen ghost, silently striking enemies' bases when they are at their weakest. And operating in the dark during a thunderstorm or mist? That’s when the immersion hits through the roof!

Or perhaps you’re just a casual player who wants to shoot bad guys and blow things up to have fun? Then, go loud, spray and pray with LMGs in broad daylight, when you can see everyone and become the spotlight for all guns pointing at you. 

Be warned though, as carelessly acting like that is not favorable in higher difficulties like Extreme, aka simulation mode. And for any hardcore, [strike]masochistic[/strike] players or Ghost Recon old-timers out there, Ghost Mode with permadeath is awaiting to challenge you. Always planning, strategically maneuvering, paying attention to your surroundings, and being precise with your bullets are the keys to enjoying GRW. Playing on Ghost Mode, Tier One (increase the challenge, earn exclusive rewards) with Extreme Difficulty, and limited HUD (Minimap, Ammo, and Items shown only) brings me back to the punishing experience of the original game. 
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2702252676
[h2]Wide Variety of Guns to Choose and Love[/h2]
GRW provides you with over a hundred firearms, with the option to carry one primary, one secondary, and one handgun, so choosing your favorite can be tough. Each gun is made distinct, not only on the model but also in the sound, both suppressed and unsuppressed. Bullet drop, recoil pattern, penetration power, and attachments contribute to that factor, too.

Gunplay is easy to learn for the most part, but hard to master if you, like me, prefer to use sniper rifles and attack from afar. Sniping over 500 meters and watching the enemies confusingly running and hiding behind cover is amusing, as they are clueless to find you since the gunshot source is too far away from them to know where to look. But if you shoot loudly about 150m close to them, they will hear, react to your shot and try to run towards the sound, so don’t camp and be on your toes.

That being said, sometimes they can magically spawn a vehicle to pursue you if you are too far away even though logically, they shouldn't know where you are, which ruins the immersion. Oddly, corpses disappear way too quickly, in under 30 seconds. The fact that you can't carry them around to hide or dump in a trash can [spoiler]where they belong to[/spoiler] feels unpolished and lackluster in a AAA tactical shooter like GRW.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2702271902
[h2]Jolly Cooperation[/h2]
GRW allows you to co-op with your friends or resort to public matchmaking to find randoms, so you can role-play together or have some dumbass ruin your plan by not communicating and exposing your position. The best thing about the co-op is that no matter where you and your friends are, all players’ progress contributes to each other. This means you can operate on one side of the map, while another player is at an airport over 15km away, to steal a resource plane and fly to the finish point. All of the players in the match will receive the same rewards.

[h1][b]Final rating: 8.5/10[/b][/h1]
Overall, it’s a solid installment to the franchise. Without all the changes in this game compared to the original, I probably wouldn’t have had a memorable and immersive experience, with over hundreds of hours of role-playing as the Ghost and exploring this recreated Bolivia. Wait for the occasional sale, even if you intend to play as leisurely as I do.

I love this game to death. 
The Bolivia setting is beautiful, the gameplay is genuinely so much fun and gives you so much freedom, and the story itself isn't bad either. HOWEVER, Modern Hardware 8 years newer than this game will often see frame drops and VERY LONG initial loading times.

If you have a modern Intel processor (12th Gen/Alder Lake i5 or newer), the game will likely fail to boot. The culprit is the 8-year-old Anti-Cheat code. It doesn't handle modern hybrid CPU architecture, so it usually just goes sour trying to launch the game.

To fix it on Intel, you must manually disable E-Cores in your BIOS or force the game to only use P-Cores via Task Manager or Process Lasso. i3s and older CPUs without E-Cores are immune. On top of that, Hyper-Threading causes stupidly long loading times across both Intel and AMD systems, so disabling Hyper-Threading/SMT helps get past the launch screen faster.

Instead of Ubisoft fixing this, they sell you a 'definitive edition' worth some $80 with content that used to be free. A DLC that just bundles content you used to be able to unlock for free, but completely ignores outdated anti-cheat code making a game we paid for unplayable.

Gameplay was and always will be great. Great game, TERRIBLE company, and an annoying propietary launcher. If you get past the politics and endure the Ubisoft launcher, Wildlands is an otherwise stellar game worth playing with friends.

[b][h1]Wild, wild, [strike]west[/strike] Bolivia[/h1][/b]
Ubisoft™ has a massive hard-on for a lot of things. But you will notice that those things are usually either open-world games or anything they can slap a Tom Clancy™ logo on.

Tom Clancy's™ Ghost Recon: Wildlands™ is your standard fare Ubisoft™ Open World Third-Person Military Espionage Stealth Action Shooter game set in an exotic backdrop where you, an operative with years and years of experience, are deployed to do some hardcore balls-to-the-wall "operators operating operationally" type of missions.

Now that sounds pretty fudmuckering exciting. And it bloody well is, for the first few hours of the game.

As you go on and learn the mechanics, the lay of the land and how you fit in, the story unfolds before you.

I won't talk much about the story but if you've ever watched any kind of spy / war / drug war films or at least played Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell™ series, you'll pretty much know what I mean. (EXCEPT THE STEALTH OPTIONS ARE MINIMAL)

You got two primary weapons, a sidearm, a drone and 3 AI companions that you can dress up use as meat shields. You can change their gender too if that's something you were looking to do. You could now be the military equivalent of the Spice Girls™ if you really wanted to. But clothing options are limited to mostly military themed stuff.

Personally, I put everyone in Ghillie Suits because it looks ridiculous but at the same time it also looks kinda cool as you stalk the forested areas, picking off targets one by one with a suppressed sniper rifle.

The gunplay mechanics feel a lot like they do in Tom Clancy's: The Division™ and Tom Clancy's: The Division 2™

Except you won't generally run into too many bullet sponge-esque enemies early in the game. Those come around later when you start fighting targets that are a bit more armored. 

The animations feel a little dated but they still look good and the addition of a photomode makes it so that you can take pictures of your operator operating operationally for whatever reason. 

Co-op is of course fun with friends because you're all trying to get to a unified goal and the journey getting there is pretty fun. Doing it with randoms is a mixed bag and your mileage may vary.

There is a lot to do in the game and sometimes it might feel like a chore but I really liked how most of the things you do will always contribute to the overall scheme of things.

Intimidate that thug? The word gets to his boss that he's a bitch-ass culero and he has to get his dick shot off.

Steal a helicopter full of drugs, guns and other miscellaneous supplies? The underboss gets his ass spanked with a nail board. Presumably.

It all adds up until the boss of the bosses of that area comes out and you get to ruin his day by either killing or capturing his ass. Results may vary.

You should give this game a shot but only under three conditions.

1. It has to be on sale.
2. You can afford like 2 McChickens™ cause that's usually the cost.
3. You are willing to spend for the cost of said McChickens™ to get the game.

If you wanted a numerical rating cause that's the sort of thing you are in to (I'm not kink shaming you.)

I would rate this game at an 8/10. As you can see from my playtime, I got to about 50-ish hours of play from what amounts to literally McChicken™ money.

Sure, I could have gotten a literal McChicken™ instead but eating that same thing for 50 hours compared to playing this game for an accumulated 50 hours, you kinda get which one I'd rather be doing.

After playing 500+ hours, I'm still having a hard time formulating an opinion about this game.

On one hand, it's a fun and engaging tactical shooter that offers plenty of replay value, thanks to it's coop feature, wide range of character customization (so many role-playing options!) and a vast open world. It's a game that let's you make your own fun, and I think it's the main reason why I've played it so much.

On the other hand, I can't say it's a good Ghost Recon game. Ubisoft seems to be making a habit of pushing their flagship franchises through the same gameplay format, which is "big open world, filled with collectibles upgrades and boring codex entries". In short - Wildlands doesn't feel any different from Far Cry, Watchdogs, The Division or Assassin's Creed. It's a "You've seen one, you've seen them all" type of situation. I'd dare say that Wildlands has an identity crisis. It doesn't really know what it wants to be, especially with the Narco Road DLC (seriously, what the hell is even that?).

I expected this game to be a more casual version of ARMA, but it turned out to be a militaristic GTA, since most of the random players you'll come across will be playing it like that. No strategy, forward-planning or teamwork whatsoever. But if you find people, who actually try to approach each situation with strategy and cunning, you may have a lot of fun.

Honestly, I'd like to downvote this game, but the 500+ hours I've played weren't because someone had a gun to my head, so I guess I enjoyed it for the most part - just not for the reasons I wanted to.

I can't think of a better description for thsi game or a better indicator or whether or not you will enjoy it. If you like the Mercenaries series and/or Metal Gear Solid V, this game is right up your alley. [b]I play purely solo[/b] and here's what I think of the game.

[b]What I like: [/b]
[*] Huge open world with wide varieties of terrain.
[*] Progress the plot at your own pace.
[*] No Restrictions. Go out and do what you want, when you want, with whatever gun you want. 
[*] Very few stealth requirement missions and escort missions. It's not going to force you to play stealth all the time. Stealth is very recommended, though. 
[*] No Agenda.
[*] Operate or Obliterate. Tactical combat, or, Schwarzeneggar combat. Your choice. Although tactical combat is the much smarter choice, we can't be smart all the time.
[*] Character customization without affecting stats! You want to operate under the influence of a mustache? GO AHEAD! You want to go full tacti-cool with multicam combat shirts under plate carriers and MOLLE everywhere? Nothing is going to stop you.


[b]What I don't like:[/b]

[*] The Friendly AI. Friendly AI is totally useless and serves only to revive you when you do something stupid. They can be enhanced, but it seems to only increase the damage they can do. 
[*] The Enemy AI. The enemy AI is just as dumb as your squad and to make up for that, they have a hard time missing you with their bullets. Distance and cover don't always guarantee your safety. 
[*] Vehicle handling is wildly inconsistent and atrocious on most vehicles. You are always better off taking a helicopter or fast traveling to get somewhere. 
[*] The post-leveling leveling system, Tier One Mode, offers very little rewards for the challenge it creates. Maybe the reward is conquering the challenge for some. Developing bad habits before you unlock it can hamper you down the road. I wish it were available from the start to counter this. 
[*] There are lots of weapons to choose from but most of them are just the same old weapons from all the other shooters out there. This may be comforting to some but I like odd-ball weapons.

I remember the first time I played Ghost Recon Wildlands.
It was the spring of 2017. I was twenty-two, standing on the edge of adulthood, searching for something vast enough to get lost in.
A friend had been talking about it for weeks, and one evening, almost on a whim, I bought the disc.
But it wasn’t just a game.
It was a map to another world.
It was Wildlands.

I installed it, turned on the console, and Bolivia stretched out before me — endless mountains, dusty villages, rivers glinting under the burning sun.
I spent that whole night learning to move slowly again, to scout, to plan, to breathe before pulling the trigger.
The stealth, the firefights, the moments of pure silence broken only by the wind — it wrapped around me like a second skin.
I wasn’t playing it.
I was living it.

Then came dozens of missions, late-night raids, and quiet helicopter rides over sleeping valleys.
I learned every province, every cartel leader’s stronghold, every path over the hills.
And without any guide — just a map, a marker, and a stubborn will — I built my story, piece by piece.
It wasn’t just a playground.
It was my war.
It was home.

Every now and then, my closest friends would join me.
We weren’t soldiers.
We were just tired kids looking for something bigger than ourselves.
I still remember those perfect moments — when the plan went wrong, when the alarm blared, when everything turned to chaos — and we laughed like madmen, scrambling to survive.
We didn’t need perfect runs.
We needed memories.
It was our refuge.
It was our bond.

And now, eight years later, I go back.
The world has changed. I have changed. I’m thirty-one now.
And those friends? They’ve moved away, chasing dreams in different cities.

Yet every time I boot up Wildlands, it’s like stepping into a painting no one else can see.
The graphics are softer now, the servers quieter — but the heart is untouched.
Every sunset, every thunderstorm, every whispered radio call speaks in a language only my memory knows.
It’s the heartbeat of another life.
It’s the breath of a world where we were unstoppable.

Ghost Recon Wildlands isn’t just a game.
It’s a time machine.
It’s a second chance to feel free, to feel fearless, to feel alive.

And as the rotors whir over the endless horizon, I remain there.
Fingers on the controller...
And a tear I cannot tell — whether it’s sorrow or gratitude.

[code]Ghost Recon Wildlands offers a lot of open world content for fans of tactical shooters and is especially enjoyable as a coop game, however, it also gets repetitive very quickly and suffers from occasional technical problems[/code]

The best way to describe [i]Wildlands[/i] is probably this: It’s a typical modern Ubisoft game, with all the strengths and weaknesses that come attached with that. On the one hand, [i]Wildlands[/i] offers a vast open world with different environments, ranging from forests to deserts to mountains. Said open world, Bolivia in this case, is also filled to the brim with content, from story missions to side activities, which are cramming up your in-game map. And of course, there are lots and lots of ways to upgrade your character: level ups, skill trees, new weapons (& weapon parts for an in-game gunsmith) to find, rebel support upgrades, etc. – in short, [i]Wildlands[/i] gives you a lot of different opportunities to invest your time.

On the other hand, the sheer mass of content also means that the developers favor quantity over the quality of the individual activities. Many of the upgrades don’t really matter – a gun I received earl in the game was better than any other gun I found throughout the rest of it. The novelty of infiltrating bases, killing high value targets or escorting them quickly wears off once you discover that [i]Wildlands[/i] basically reuses the same few mission structures throughout the entire game. And considering that even though the environments look different, many of the bases, camps and hideouts do not, all of your infiltrations or shootouts will quickly turn into a blur. Even though I spent 54h in the game to tackle all of the available story missions, I won’t be able to name even one location that stood out to me – in fact, the many, many locations you visit are so generic that I wouldn’t be able to draw you a map of even one of them.

That said, especially in coop, the basic gameplay loop works solid enough that the generic locations won’t matter much at first. It’s fun to use the variety of gadgets & approaches [i]Wildlands[/i] offers in order to accomplish objectives just the way you want. You could use a helicopter and a parachute to drop into an enemy base, barge in with a tank or sneak your way in by stealthily eliminating guards in your way. Especially the missions tasking you with killing a specific target allow for different tactics – sometimes a well-timed sniper shot from a nearby mountain is all it takes, sometimes a full-on assault with allied rebel NPCs might be a better choice.

[i]Wildlands[/i] offers two enemy factions, the Santa Blanca cartel and Unidad, which sort of work like the police in the [i]Grand Theft Auto[/i] franchise. Both factions got normal goons with guns as well as special types (snipers, armored enemies). Sometimes you’ll also encounter enemy vehicles, like helicopters or tanks. However, as the enemy variety is pretty low and vehicles are only used in certain cases (e.g. enemy convoys), they’re rarely more than simple gunfodder. If you want to infiltrate a base you might want to take of snipers first, but you won’t have to change your approach because of certain enemy types - disappointing. It would have been nice to make plans based on the enemies present, not just on the location alone.

Speaking about the variety in approaching objectives I previously praised, I also have to point it that this sadly doesn’t last forever. Especially on higher difficulty (or the “Tier One”-mode available after reaching max level), [i]Wildlands[/i] becomes a much different game. Enemies can kill you almost immediately now and their locations aren’t hinted at on the map anymore, which basically makes stealth approaches the only viable option if you want to complete missions. Considering [i]Wildlands[/i] is a tactical shooter after all, this isn’t surprising, but I’m still mentioning it for those who don’t want to sneak around guards all the time.

My biggest gripe with the stealth approaches in [i]Wildlands[/i] concerns the enemy AI, which can ruin your well-planned approaches to a mission in more ways than you expect. Throughout most of the game, the AI is solid enough: enemies aren’t particularly smart, but they do take cover when shoot at from afar and call for help if needed. What makes them so annoying in terms of stealth approaches, however, is their unpredictable spotting. Sometimes enemies are able to spot you through walls or other solid structures (the snipers in particular), sometimes they don’t react to corpses of their friends but at other times they immediately sound the alarm instead. They’re also very good at “coincidentally” heading directly to your location when searching for you: One time I had an entire truck of reinforcements spawn directly behind me even though it was only my coop partner they spotted. These AI issues can make stealth approaches quite frustrating, especially as mission checkpoints can be quite bad as well.

Anyway, even while stealth doesn’t work as well as it should be, getting spotted is less frustrating when you got a coop partner to help you out: [i]Wildlands[/i] opens up a lot more if you got friends to play with. Especially on lower difficulty, you can simply go wild while approaching missions, which is a lot of fun. Maybe one of you is piloting a helicopter transporting another, who is using a sniper to take out a target from above. Or you’re participating in a great car chase, with one player driving while the other is trying to take down your pursuers. But even on higher difficulties it’s really entertaining to infiltrate a base with each player taking care of a different corner and I can’t think of many games allowing for all these moments at once.

That said, while the generic locations and missions as well as the general repetitiveness of [i]Wildlands[/i] don’t feel as bad if you play this game in coop and I highly recommend playing this game with friends, coop also comes with additional problems. These are mainly of the technical sort, like progress sometimes not being properly saved when finishing missions together. Especially the “Silent Spade” mission was bugged, with me receiving the rewards for finishing the mission together while my coop partner was stuck at an earlier checkpoint according to the game. Additionally, while the game ran fine once connected, we encountered many issues trying to join each other’s lobby. This might be thanks to Ubisoft Connect, which is required if you want to play this game – online or not.

Lastly, let’s talk about the story of [i]Wildlands[/i]. The basic set-up of [i]Wildlands[/i] is basically to take down a big bad cartel boss, however, in order to approach him you have to take down a dozen of his underlings first. Of course, it shouldn’t be surprising that the story of [i]Wildlands[/i] is quite cliched and doesn’t feel very coherent, as you can tackle the story missions in any order you want. Considering you also don’t encounter the big bad until the final mission, apart from a handful of previous voice lines, the big villain doesn’t receive much characterization beyond “he’s evil”. Frankly, the entire story set-up feels like it’s just window-dressing for the open world activities anyway, so don’t expect it to be more than that.

Concluding, [i]Wildlands[/i] does offer a solid gameplay loop that’s especially great when experienced with friends. But it also suffers from a problem of quantity over quality, which might lead to a few fun hours at first but a feeling of boredom later on. The longer you play, the more you realize that [i]Wildlands[/i] is lacking depth and some true variety. It’s fun but for a tactical shooter, it's also a bit mindless and might be best experienced with some long breaks between sessions.

You might find a lot of people in this review section saying the game's main downside is the fact that Ubisoft made it, and I agree completely; it's the one factor that stops this game from being a fantastic open-world FPS.

Don't get me wrong, this is still an absolute banger, but it didn't go without it's bumps in the road. Upon release, many glitches were prominent, which definitely stabbed the game's performance early on where it's most critical. But as time goes on, things got fixed, and people moved on to the next thing as the game got its repairs. This left it to not really blow up as much as what could be expected. I mean you look at the game firsthand and you hear glitches and Ubisoft, already a no-go, right?

What the game lacks in some functionality it makes up for in visual beauty. Yeah, you do need a decent rig to run it smoothly, but it's absolutely worth it. It still stuns me now, and I've tried RTX Minecraft. The lush forests, barren saltflats, and changing weather really bring this game to life.
There's LOTS, and I mean LOTS of information in the game about Bolivia itself which I find to be extremely appealing to have. Many games will take place in like France or something and not give you ANY information about the culture. That doesn't slide here. In the game, you're an operative in a country that isn't immediately in the mainstream media, so if you aren't familiar, the game gives you trivia. Post-war Germans living in the country, Death Road, Jesús Malverde, and more stories are able to be found. There are also PLENTY of files and dialogue on the main game story as well in case that's what you want to pay attention to, but none of said files and trivia are required to continue on. It's a respectful thing to do, and it shows the developers really went out of their way to understand Bolivian culture; it shows how much they really cared about the game, so it's nice to see.

The stealth in this game is fairly good, def could be better but pretty good. The game lacks in being able to drag bodies which is a pretty big letdown, but usually the AI is pretty easy anyways. The easiness was actually a complaint early on for the game, so Ubisoft added Extreme mode and Ghost Mode. Extreme mode meaning your body would seize if you breathed too much, and Ghost Mode meaning basically 2 shots without a revive and you gotta start over. All the way over. Like, back to the part where you're landing in the country, over. Talk about being careful. Still, can't drag bodies which is annoying and I really wish being able to hide in bushes was a bit more functional than it is as of writing, but the enemy on the right difficulty can still be scary at times which makes it all the more satisfying to do things right. When playing with friends, I like to have my friends infiltrate compounds while I post up as a sniper correcting any mistakes they make from 400+ meters away.

It would be a crime to not talk about the guns in a gun game. The guns are great in their models and customization. You can paint your guns solid colors, official camos, funny camos, whatever suits you. Then you can modify it to just how you like. Every Buchon has a custom gun you unlock too that reflects their personality. For example, one guy you capture builds submarines, so naturally his unlock is a gun made from sub parts. The sniper rifles were done really well in my opinion because every rifle has quite a different bullet drop, and since the landscape is huge, you have to pay attention to it a lot. I found myself testing different scopes with different rifles to see which was best, and started remembering where the range was on each set. It's very satisfying to get it right and pull off a 500+ meter shot.

The customization on the clothes as well is really good. The game gives you hundreds of options if you want to go with tactical clothes or more civilian-style like Nomad's base character. Of course, there's like 70 something different colors you can do for basically half or more of those clothing options too. When you're done with that, you can choose what patches you want to do on your backpack, baseball cap, shoulder-armor, etc. "Made in the 757" is a personal fav.

I'm a motorhead, so obviously I want the driving mechanics to be good. This game did okaaaay with that, but honestly better quite a few other games out there. Steering is pretty annoying, but the transmission mechanic is really good. You can hear the RPM climbing and, if you're smart, tap the throttle before it shifts to get a premature gearshift in the car. I'm glad they paid attention to that. What didn't go so well was the flying mechanics. The flying, like driving, is okaaaay, at least in classic mode. If you want to hit something in classic mode with weapons, forget it. It's basically impossible. Ubisoft tried to fix this issue with new flying mechanics but they found a way to realllllly fumble it. It's REALLY bad. Driving = eh, not bad | flying = pretty trash depending on what you're doing.

Pros:

+ Graphics are beautiful looking
+ Sounds are amazing from walking to firing off different weapons
+ Guns and using the Gunsmith
+ Open world and you can do any mission is any order you want to
+ A good story, but based more on investigations and missions rather than just pure dialogue (e.g. RP games).
+ Background information about Bolivia and that a lot of it is based on actual facts
+ Customizations 


Neutral:

*/- Stealth
*/- Camouflage 


Cons:

-  AI at times makes you question their intelligence
- Driving a car can feel like you’re constantly playing a drifting simulator
- Crashes that happen once in a while when playing co-op


The story really isn’t a story, but about missions with slight background knowledge about who you need to take out. You hardly know anything about who you are, who your operatives that you work with are, or who your boss is and know very little about even the organization you work for. They made the story more or less to investigation and/or criminal solving shows (Law and Order, Criminal Minds, etc.) in sense where you finish a case and move onto the next case. In the end, you know more about the enemy than you do about yourself and/or your own operatives. They did an excellent job at executing the story in this regard, but don’t expect a big time story from games that relate more around Roleplaying titles. 

The game looks amazing. All my settings are on max and never seen any AA issues; as well never seen any stuttering or FPS drops. The grass and bushes will move or get flatten when moving over them or when in prone position so you can flatten the grass, move back slightly, and snipe people from afar. The different biomes and the weather effects with a day and night cycle makes the game feel realistic and does an accurate job (more or less based on the given Kilometers within the game) of showing off Bolivia’s landscape.

The sounds whether walking on snow, dirt, mud, or diving into the water is very noticeable. It adds to that realism compared to other games where a lot of the footing is the same regardless what biome you’re in. The voice actors do a good job at commenting about missions, syncing shots, cinematics that occur, and just bluntly describing how they’d love to ‘stick it to them’. At times they’ll throw in a joke or give some insight about where they came from and/or who they (not a lot, but at least it’s something). Vehicles in general sound different from one another; whether it’s a four door coup, to a lambo, to a pick-up truck, they all have their distinctive sounds. Both helicopters sound different from one another and the bush plane sounds like a bush plane. 

 From firing off a MP5 to a M4A1 to a G28 all sound genuine to their counterparts. Adding a compressor only makes it feel more genuine when doing stealth combat. You have an ample amount of customization for your weapons: scopes, barrels, grips, muzzles, triggers, stocks, and few other options. Each option as dozen or more items that help with accuracy, handling, rate of fire, damage, etc.; you customize your weapon based on your playstyle or how you want the weapon to feel in terms of gun n’ gun, aiming, or hip fire. Depending on how customize your weapons they’ll lean toward one direction or have a recoil higher than other weapons and they feel all very accurate based on how you fit your weapon. Also, you have multiple options to paint your weapons.

This game has kept its word about doing any province in any order you want to. I felt like this was a great aspect of the game and a feature that wasn’t a lie or falsely advertised. I went from one area to another based on certain weapons and gadgets for said weapons early on and finished other zones for pure enjoyment. You have multiple ways of transportation: cars, trucks, diesel trucks; planes, helicopters, boats, motorcycles, and parachutes. You do have to get used to flying, but once you have that in place flying becomes easier that other modern warfare titles. Some of the vehicles are horrendous when driving regardless of how fast or slow one would takes around a curve or eases on the brakes. Some of the vehicles feel like they were imported from an actual drifting game and with a lot of roads being on hills and/or trying to pursuit someone can become an absolute headache at times. 

Customization in general of your character is appealing compared to other titles that fit within this genre. You can wear sunglasses, hat, different vest types, you can wear civilian clothing and/or military clothing; you can mismatch items and numerous color variations regardless how you pick your items. When it comes to using camouflage to hide yourself from enemies, this concept goes entirely out of the window. You could be engulfed in a full ghillie suit and the enemy will still see you a few hundred meters away. This is applied if you’re in full black camouflage and in pitch darkness where they don’t have any Night Vision on and still can see you through the brush when using a compressor. I would like to see some rework on how camouflage works as this is a major factor at times when using stealth against the enemy. 

Most of the times stealth works to a degree; one can sneak up behind an enemy and eliminate them in melee or sniping them well over five hundred meters away. Factors that can hurt your stealth is noise (gunfire, running, explosions, etc.), another guard seeing the corpse of a fallen member, or being noticed because camouflage didn’t do its job. There are traits to help prevent from being detected, which at times makes it too easy (e.g. If you’re about to be spotted and you’re hundred and twenty meters away, just prone and they’ll stop noticing you). There are devices to help distract guards to your location so you can pick them off without someone else spotting their body. I would’ve liked to see an option about picking up the corpse and moving it instead of waiting a few seconds and having it magically disappear. Also, regardless of what weapon you use, you can one shot anyone as long as you’re in stealth mode. I understand this helps in co-op to do sync shots, but I feel like that this method is way too easy. If you’re not in co-op mode, sync shots with your AI counterparts are an amazing feature and it helps clear out majority of the operations you take. 

The AI at times can be the best help or the worst help. They will NOT engage unless you command them to do so or if you are under heavy amounts of fire where you will automatically command your operatives to attack. They will remain in stealth mode for majority of the time and the more you upgrade your sync shots the more use you can get out from your operatives. When they do open fire, they just seem at times not knowing how to eliminate an enemy when it really matters. There really isn’t a middle ground with your AI operatives. I’ve seen them meters away from an enemy and just eating all their bullets instead of turning around and shooting them instead. The AI does need work, but you can finish the game on a higher difficulty – just expect a headache at times dealing with them. 

I did experience some crashes when playing in co-op mode and when I finished the game (both endings). In co-op mode, if one person joins the game, then it’s you two vs Bolivia instead of two people and two AI, or three players and one AI. The AI will still talk even though they aren’t in your squad and it’s to keep the immersion within the game. I never experienced any lag or disconnects when playing with my friends, but the crashes would happen randomly. Co-op needs work, but when it does work it is an amazing experience with friends. 

I recommend buying this title to play with your friends. Unfortunately, I can't add any more information - I exceeded the amount.

(Update under initial review) Nice game if you like open world games like Far Cry, GTA, RDR2. You're a CIA asset who is dropped in Bolivia and get assigned a squad, your objective is to take down a criminal syndicate that spans multiple regions with bosses and gangs. You collect resources, find clues, upgrade weapons and skills and such. The map is vast and diverse. Having citizen NPCs everywhere makes the world come alive. Game runs at at least 60fps with all ultra on a 5900x + RTX3080. No need to install on SSD, game loads fast enough from HDD. Game + DLC pack is on sale for €15 at the moment of writing, a really good deal.

- Update after playing for multiple hours now. The map is incredibly large and diverse, but also diverse on macro scale. There are salt planes, deserts, mountains, temperate forests, tropical jungles for example, all with their own weather patterns and scene lighting. There are unique buildings with beautiful architecture and interiors. As you progress and did some investigations the background story comes alive, while a rebel army starts to form. I've seen pretty intense fights. - Another nice detail, vehicles do not unspawn the moment you step in another vehicle or look the other way for a brief moment. So you may arrive with a car near a town, do your business, and an hour later you walk back to your parked car (though sometimes friendly NPCs "borrow" your vehicle). There are also really funny interactions between NPCs. For example, one mobster is a famous singer, you can visit his mansion. On the street there can be fans who are annoying a guard with their cheering. - Anyway, the game is incredibly big with tons of missions and side quests. There are four main routes with unique story missions to get to the big boss, but you only need two of those main routes, so you can complete the story any way you want it.

Here's the easiest way to put this.

Imagine The Division, but no bullet sponges, add vehicles and aircraft.

The game is squad focused, encourages stealth (sometimes requires it), is the highest tiers of play... being smart, tactical, and extremely accurate is highly important.

It's a good game.

90% of this game is extremely fun.

10% of it can be summarized with some excerpts from the Sam Fisher mission:

NOMAD, THIS IS MATCHWOOD. HERE ARE MY COORDINATES.

MISSION FAILED: YOU LEFT THE MISSION AREA [that you weren't in].

NOMAD, THIS IS MATCHWOOD. HERE ARE MY COORDINATES.

MISSION FAILED: YOU LEFT THE MISSION AREA [that you still weren't in].

NOMAD, THIS IS MATCHWOOD. HERE ARE MY COORDINATES.

MISSION FAILED: TARGET KILLED [no one in your squad had weapons drawn].

NOMAD, THIS IS MATCHWOOD. HERE ARE MY COORDINATES.

[Restart game because some of your co-op team mates have their clocks de-synced from yours suddenly, and only one of you now has this mission].

The game is mostly solid, and mostly fun, but when it doesn't work, it REALLY does not work. Enemies will randomly see you through multiple layers of concrete and metal, or drill you in the same centimeter ring on your head with a helicopter mounted minigun with zero wind-up time. The game will test you, and not always in a good way -  your patience will definitely be pushed to the limit, and the immersion you feel for most of the game will stutter over and over again, as you become enraged at Ubisoft's inability to code consistently (or in the case of the Sam Fisher mission or anything requiring you to not kill targets and suffer random failures because, from what I can only assume, someone off in another part of the world died of natural causes and because their loved ones were there to see them off, Ghost squad was detected).

One additional set of gripes is the notion of shared stealth - again, in another part of the world, a player does something to become detected - hundreds of kilometers to the east, suddenly an enemy base of a totally different faction is alerted to you, and suddenly sends pinpoint accurate mortars in your direction despite no one reasonably being able to even know you were there. FEELS GHOSTY.

I still recommend this game on sale, but it'll make you consistently angry enough to not buy the DLC and to seriously reconsider putting money into future iterations of this or other Tom Clancy games, so take that for what it's worth. These aren't even difficult things to have considered (or fixed), so if you're like me it will really give you pause when reaching for your wallet.

I have put more hours on console in this game than I have here, but let me say that since launch, this game has never become dull. There is SO much replayablility when it comes to this game. Not only that, I feel that anyone with any play style can easily enjoy this game. Whether that is going in with the biggest, loudest guns, to sneaking around an entire military base taking everyone out, to doing the most ridiculous this you can possibly think of and execute. 

When it comes to customization, this game does it so well. You can make your person look completely badass or extremely ridiculous and goofy. You can also make your weapons look AND play the way you'd like! You can change the different skins on them, and even customize how each skin would look on your weapon. There are also a ton of weapon mods you can find around the map that will help you build the perfect weapon and loadout for whatever play-through you want!

When it comes to difficulty, you can change it throughout your playthough to give you more of a challenge. From arcade difficulty (the easiest), to simply enjoy the setting and the story of the game to permadeath, where you get one primary weapon and one secondary and can play with no HUD and lose all progress upon death.

Glitches with multiplayer, lobbies, matchmaking, missions showing checkpoints that don't exist (on SP and MP) appear out of nowhere. So thanks for nothing on that one.

Narco Road comes out. This is Ubioft's method of taking the very brand that is Ghost Recon...spreading it out on a table...and SKULL RAPEING IT FOR ALL TO SEE.

Well, clearly I like this game if you take a look at my time played. So I figured it's probably worth leaving a review in case you were considering getting this. First, a look at why I purchased the game. 

I really wanted a game where I could take my time and play as an overwatch marksman and just snipe people, which Wildlands offers in abundance. At the time Sniper GW 3 wasn't out and the Sniper Elite franchise has a story that is on rails. 

Wildlands is open world with absolutely beautiful scenery. The game looks flat out amazing. Weapon graphics, clothing, vehicles, and the world all have amazing graphics. If you fire at the same target from different distances, the bullet holes will look different. It's incredibly well done in that regard. Physics include bullet drop. AI accounts for rain and night time. It really does offer an immersion if that is what you want. Or you can become rambo and use an LMG as you walk through explosions. There is a true variety to how you play AND the games tracks it. It records stats and gives you a game style based on your preference. I have personally played as Overwatch and Ranger, though I am not sure what the requirements are for these titles after 200 hours.

The story is interesting overall. If you are OCD like me and you unlock literally everything, you get to read and listen to a lot of the pieces to the story that piece together somewhat of a puzzle. That said, the missions are really repetitive. The rebel missions are the same, finding skill points and weapons doesn't change throughout the game. The only real joy you will get after a while is doing the story missions just so you get something different coming your way. The cut-scenes are in the same building, but the dialogue and action make it very interesting.

Gameplay. Ah, the gameplay. Driving is weird. It's really cool how all vehicles handle differently with some excelling in certain areas like off-roading, but the overall control can be hard to get used to at first. Flying is very fun and you can get quite high to do a HALO jump in, if that's your thing. You can upgrade your character to run further, quieter, through explosions, and bouncing bullets depending on what you upgrade first. If you collect everything there are more than enough skill points to upgrade everything for the perfect soldier. However you can't upgrade running into these areas where you literally get stuck. In true Ubisoft fasion there are places everywhere that you just get stuck in. Even in the gaming world where new titles constantly clamor for attention, Wildlands still shines. Its polished graphics and immersive open-world environment feel just as fresh today as when we first dove in. The attention to detail in the sprawling landscapes, from dense jungles to arid deserts, is simply stunning.

But what truly makes Wildlands a standout experience is its co-op play. Playing with friends turned the game into a rollercoaster of hilarity, tactical brilliance, and occasional friendly fire mishaps. Whether we were coordinating helicopter assaults on drug cartel compounds or hijacking convoys, every mission was an adventure.

The outposts and objectives could sometimes seem repetitive, but when you're laughing your head off with buddies while trying to stay stealthy, it hardly matters. And speaking of variety, the game's high weapon customizability and the abundance of character perks added depth and replayability, keeping us hooked for hours on end.

Ghost Recon Wildlands isn't just a game; it's a canvas for unforgettable co-op stories. It's a testament to the power of friendship, teamwork, and the joy of conquering challenging missions together. If you're looking for a game that stands the test of time and offers endless opportunities for cooperative fun, look no further than Ghost Recon Wildlands. It's an experience that I'll cherish for years to come.

[h1]A massive highly re-playable gorgeous co-optional open world (stealth?) experience[/h1]
[i]A tremendous update to the first game, awesome fun solo and great with a friend(or 3!)[/i]

While a caveat is necessary regarding the current server behaviour when trying to start up a co-op session, being an older title [b]Ubisoft[/b] has put this guy onto some sort of aged hobbly decrepit cranky server listing, meaning starting a co-op session requires intense patience. The trick is to wait until the in game store is accessible on both Sessions before attempting to join...

Which leads into the second seemingly negative sounding statement regarding this SUPERB title. The DLC and in game stores are both just horrible. The DLC [i](Narco Road & Fallen Ghosts)[/i] actually require a completely SEPERATE toon! Meaning your main game character is not used in any way, and, the writing is rather naff on both of them. [i]Avoid[/i]. The in game store allows for "boosting" XP and credits and weapons, avoid this too. Oddly, the free Ubi-Rewards give you 2 of the most powerful and in fact, overpowered weapons available in game...sooo...buy the base game and you good.

Right then, on to the cool stuff, because my god this thing is awesome:
[list]
[*] So big. 
[*] Excellent story. 
[*] Varied environments
[*] Range of uniquely performing weaponry
[*] Multitude of gameplay / mission completion options.
[*] Can take as long or as short as you want to finish
[*] Cool hidden stuff.
[*] BASE jumpiiiiiiiiiiiiiiing!!!
[/list]
The Chilean peninsula this game is situated in is Fictional, but based on superb real world research that includes wildly differing regions varying from Andean snowcapped Alpine peaks to humid swamps and heavily wooded rolling hills, all with industry and town locations fitting to their regions.

This accentuates the background to a rather excellent storyline which is wonderfully voice acted and I presume mo-capped. The production values are impressive across the board in this regard.

While it is clear many locations have buildings copy/pasted, their interiors and exteriors are all individual removing "repeated dungeon" fatigue common to many titles. The indistinguishable primary bases scattered throughout this world sized....world immerse one even further.

The World itself really feels alive with AI citizens wandering around on foot, plane, train or automobile and commenting on story driven events, alongside radio broadcasts setting the scene and enemies commenting on their lives and postings or patrols. All have reactionary based animations and behaviours. Your squad even comments on regions you enter, adding further to the experience.
[hr][/hr]
Combat AI is...an interesting one. Depending on your difficulty level which ramps up dramatically if you choose the endgame ranking system in order to unlock more toys, skins and cosmetics, you can end up in one shot instadead territory if discovered. Which does bring forward the GHOST intended nature of the game, you are not really meant to be seen at any point!

One can however, allow full degeneration into CQC combat, but the realism kicks in here with you being as squishy as most of the enemies. First shot wins. While playing with the AI teammates who are essentially gods and effectively give you a "life" (later 2) if you are downed, your Co-Op experience will vary in this regard. If your idiot buddy stirs a hornets nest, it really is best to run and hide to return to resurrect them, or let the timer run out and they teleport back.

Death merely loses you your most recent XP, resources and objectives earned before the last autosave. Autosaves occur on Teleportation, and entry into fresh combat zones, so its pretty good in that regard.

Avoiding all that is done by playing the game as intended. Careful reconnoitring of the objective, enemy patrol patterns, resources and backup potential allow you to select your infiltration point be it via BASE, HALO, ground assault or even using the Rebels to attack and distract.

The Rebels you are assisting can be used to call in Mortar Strikes, entire backup squads, auto-recon, or do distraction attacks on command. Your squad, can also to a degree be controlled in this manner, sending them to specific points, holding zones or going stealth or full combat.

This leads to the coolest feature of the game, Synchronised Shots. Sync shots with AI are a bit overpowered and can be used to reach all sorts of locations, while doing it in co-op is a lot more satisfying and a true art form. Marking targets, you then wait until all are lined up for their shots and call a simultaneous hit dropping them all without alerting the remaining enemies. Very effective.

While the better weapons and attachments are hidden across the entire map, usually in Points Of Interest, some are inside main bases or mission areas. One can attack mission bases outside of the Mission to gain access to the loot, and when you return on the Mission you'll find enemy layouts and triggers dramatically different. POI's are not required to be fully cleared to complete the game, unless you enable the endgame scoring system in which case you'll be hunting for every advantage possible!

To be clear, [b]Tier One[/b] (endgame scoring) is totally optional, and just ramps up the difficulty while forcing you to then invest in upgrading your weapons to match enemy armour levels. A bit of fun and not terribly complicated, but totally unnecessary to finish the game.

The Rebel Leader, Pat Katari is a bit of a miserable qunt. Whenever you do call the chap to drop in a vehicle for you, the clown will do his best to confound you by placing your called in item either halfway up a cliff face, in the middle of traffic, or on top of an entire enemy squad. This feature though is best used when clear of obvous pitfalls where it then behaves as intended, and makes for trudging your way on foot from a random location you found yourself in, back to civilisaton far less tedious (or just teleport to a base...but break your immersion).

[h1]Overall, one of my most favourite gaming experiences. Highly recommended both solo and if you can find a friend who isnt a gung-ho looney![/h1]

[h1] This is the peak Ghost Recon game. [/h1]
All of the best qualities make up this [b] perfect [/b] 3rd person shooter: story-telling, gameplay, stealth mechanics, and a lively world filled with NPCs and other components that make you actually feel like you're in Bolivia. 

Don't even bother buying/downloading Breakpoint, GR should have stopped at this masterpiece. On its own, Wildlands truly makes you feel like an operative behind enemy lines; working to defeat a dangerous cartel with the help of rebel cells. This game includes a compelling story line, along with memorable characters and scenes that will make you come back year after year to replay it. And when it's all over? There are plenty of side quests and locations to keep you engaged.

The gameplay is what truly sets this apart from other 3rd person shooters, in that there are tons of ways to take on enemies or explore the terrain.  From driving APCs through the front gate of a Santa Blanca outpost to scaling mountains under the cover of darkness, you will surely enjoy your time playing Ghost Recon Wildlands.

Despite some problems and strange design oversights, Ghost Recon Wildlands feels like a Ghost Recon game to me again. I know, I know. Everyone says it doesn’t feel like Ghost Recon. I contend that this difference of opinion is due to the fact that Wildlands gives you the freedom to make of it what you will, meaning that patience and tactical behavior are choices rather than enforced gameplay mechanics. 

First, I should say that Wildlands is gorgeous. I have a reasonably decent rig (GTX 970 FTW, i5 4690k @ 4.2 GHz, 16 GB RAM), and I was able to run the game on a mixture of mostly high and very high settings at a comfortable framerate after Ubi’s performance patches. I typically got at or near 60 FPS in most situations, though the game does dip uncomfortably often into the 40s in areas with heavy vegetation, many enemies or effects, or both. There are also periodic mini-freezes in which the game locks up for no apparent reason for 10 seconds or more, only to resume right where you left off as if nothing happened. These hitches are frustrating, but not game breaking. 

Your soldier’s character animations ooze military authenticity, the many varied environments of Bolivia are both rugged and absolutely beautiful, and detail is evident in every part of the game. Lay down in a salt flat, for instance, and your character will stand up with chalky white powder on his uniform. Use your guns for too long, and they will begin to show paint scratching and wear until you refresh their paint. Thick grass sways in the wind, dust blows across arid mountains and deserts, and glimmering rivers wind their ways across the landscape.

Bolivia is enormous and massively varied. Whereas other Ghost Recon games tended to pick one type of climate (then ask you to purchase expansions providing new environments), Wildlands offers a startling array of environmental diversity. There are jungles, plains, farms, swamps, mountains, arid hills, deserts, salt flats, canyons, pine forests—the list goes on. All of these environments are fantastically crafted to feel both rugged and convincing. Many of these environments promote certain playstyles. Lush jungles, for instance, make it hard to snipe effectively into bases, leading players to sneak up to enemy compounds in the thick vegetation. Arid mountains, on the other hand, provide little concealment on approach to a base and offer interesting geographic challenges, encouraging players to scout and engage from a distance.

If there’s a problem with Wildlands’ Bolivia, it’s that it is sometimes too big. Roads are often jagged and windy, meaning that the most efficient way to travel is almost always by helicopter. As a result, I found myself spending a lot of my time fast traveling between various safehouses until I could find one with a helicopter. Maybe that’s a good thing; sticking to established roads would mean missing most of the backcountry glory of Wildlands’ environments. But beautiful environments notwithstanding, travel in Wildlands can be a hassle. 

The overarching story is a bit simplistic (dismantle a drug cartel), but each of the game's dozens of provinces has a smaller, more interesting backstory behind it that feeds into the larger strategic objective. In one province, I was tasked with finding and capturing a man who makes the bodies of the cartel’s victims disappear by tracking a “death truck” as it made its morbid rounds. In another province, I had to hunt down and kill a former U.S. soldier who was taking a paycheck to train cartel foot soldiers. In still another, I had to track and assassinate two sadistic cartel torturers. I found the vast majority of these mini-stories much more compelling than the overall narrative, and it was satisfying to really feel like I was helping take apart a massively complex criminal organization one piece at a time. 

How you play Wildlands will have a large impact on how much you enjoy your time with the game. At its best in the hands of a patient team of players, the game feels like a brilliant reimagining of the old SOCOM and GRAW games. There are few things more satisfying than taking the time to recon a large enemy base using a small drone, planning a route to the objective, then slipping in quietly and efficiently without setting off an alarm. In these tactical, stealthy scenarios, the game is absolutely brilliant. 

However, with the exception of a handful of inta-fail stealth missions, Wildlands does not require players to play tactically. There are few penalties for simply setting off an alarm—something that can happen as easily as missing a shot on bad guy or dropping someone whose body is in plain view of his friends—because the difficulty of the game is lacking. Even on Extreme, the game feels too forgiving. As a result, players have little incentive to worry much about making mistakes or planning tactically. Instead, most of my experiences with the game in co-op amounted to all-out assaults on enemy bases. That might be fine for some folks, but I think it accentuates Wildlands’ weaknesses. 

Wildlands feels amazing as a stealthy tactical shooter, but marginal at best as an action-packed third-person shooter. It’s very clear that the game was designed to be played tactically, and it is fantastically enjoyable and satisfying when that playstyle is adopted. But when players decide to go Rambo, the game feels clunky and awkward and unimpressive. Given how often I saw players adopting the latter approach, it’s no surprise that many of them find the game lacking. They simply aren’t playing it as it was meant to be played.

Truthfully, though, the tendency to just go nuts is probably not the fault of the players. Wildlands makes no real effort to enforce or even encourage tactical play. Most shooters like this one allow players to play them like Call of Duty if they so choose, but those players understand that such tactics will likely result in death and mission failure. Not so in Wildlands. Similarly, a lot of games have adopted mission rating structures (bronze, silver, gold, etc.) that allow players to do whatever they want, but require thoughtful play to achieve higher rankings. Not so in Wildlands. Still other shooters allow players who, like me, tend to restart missions when stealth is broken to reload a checkpoint and try again. Not so in Wildlands. Instead, players have to commit suicide or leave the game in order to reset to a checkpoint. 

As a result, the ability of tactically minded players to truly enjoy Wildlands will come down to their ability to maintain discipline on their own without any external prompting or encouragement. The same goes for any players they join in co-op. I quickly found that the latter option was all but impossible, so I was faced with a stark choice: stick to solo, where I could control the playstyle and pace of the game but was saddled with questionably useful AI teammates and severely limited order options, or take my chances in co-op knowing that it likely would devolve into an over-the-shoulder shooting gallery. I often chose the solo route. The game was still enjoyable that way—enough so that I think tactical single players will like Wildlands just fine. But I desperately wished for deeper tactical options with my AI team (individual orders, anyone?), and I couldn’t escape the feeling of lost potential. With some different design choices, Wildlands could have been the tactical co-op experience of the generation. No such luck.

All things considered, I greatly enjoyed my time with Wildlands. Played correctly, it is easily on par with the Advanced Warfighter games. While the gameplay is similar throughout, that gameplay is strong enough and the environments diverse enough that the game stayed fresh for me all the way through the roughly 65 hours it took me to complete it. If you're into tactical play, you should definitely check this one out.

[h1] Introduction. [/h1]
Good day, dear users of the Steam playground. More than 90 hours later, I decided to write a review about the game itself.
I am one of those who completed Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon® Wildlands 100%, collecting intelligence from all operations. I managed to beat the game on difficulty level [b] "Ultimate" (highest difficulty level) [/b] and reached [b] 20 Tier [/b]. It took a lot of time and patience to complete all the additional tasks. I think I'm ready to tell you about it. Let's get started!

[h1] Plot. [/h1]
The game is set in [b] Bolivia [/b]. The supplies are controlled by the [b] Santa Blanca [/b] cartel, a powerful organization whose influence is destabilizing the region. The head of the organization is [spoiler] El Suenho [/spoiler] or [b] "Dreamer" [/b]. By hiring the best specialists, his organization has become the largest drug supplier in the world. [b] Santa Blanca [/b] managed to bribe the army, police and politicians. Due to the lack of protection, the Bolivian people began to lose hope for a happy future.
The US government is concerned about the growing influence of the cartel. As a result, [b] the United States Army [/b] sends an elite squad [b] "Ghosts" [/b] to uncover the connection between drug dealers and the local government and destroy the cartel.

[h1] Gameplay. [/h1]
You will take the role of one of the members of the "Ghosts" squad, and the CIA agent [spoiler] Karen Bowman [/spoiler] will be in charge of the "Regicide" operation. Your main task is to get to the "Dreamer". But this is not as easy as it seems. First, we have to disable each of the four departments of the cartel. And to get to them, you need to catch their assistants.
Think it's that simple? No matter how it is! To get to the assistants, you need to catch all the employees who play their role. Take the Production Department, for example, where each minion completes a different phase in the production of cocaine.
You will not be alone. Local rebels led by [spoiler] Amaru [/spoiler] and [spoiler] Paka Katari [/spoiler] will come to the rescue. However, their support will be extremely small and not very effective. You have to complete various secondary tasks scattered across all areas.
However, it is not the cartel people who are afraid, but the [spoiler] of the Unity soldiers [/spoiler]. These guys are much more dangerous than militants, they have good equipment and excellent equipment. These guys can screw up your operation by calling for help. Then you just have to run and not get caught in their eyes.
You can also meet heroes from other projects "Ubisoft": help [spoiler] "Rainbow-6" [/spoiler] find [spoiler] Saveiro [/spoiler], ensure [spoiler] Sam Fisher [/spoiler] security and conduct a joint operation with [spoiler] John Kozak [/spoiler] from the game Ghost Recon: Future Soldier.
You can also meet the well-known [spoiler] "Predator" [/spoiler] from a series of films.
In addition to the cooperative mode, there is PvP content, starting with the [spoiler] "Ghost War" [/spoiler] mode and ending with the [spoiler] "Battle Royale" [/spoiler]. However, it is very difficult to find people in these modes, and their development was stopped long ago. There is a chance to find a match. 

[b] Advantages: [/b]
[list]
    [*] Open world. You will see stunning and varied landscapes, from impenetrable swamps to snow-capped mountains. Most of the world is wilderness. That is, you will have to move on roads and off-road, by air and by water. Along the way, you can meet wild animals that complement the locations.
    [*] Special effects. Bright explosions, dirt on clothes and blood splatters after a shot perfectly complement the surroundings. However, that was not even what I liked. Try walking through the jungle during thunderstorms. Get a lot of positive emotions.
    [*] Personalization. We play for [spoiler] Nomad [/spoiler], but no one forbids changing his appearance or equipment. Maybe there are not hundreds of settings, but you can make your fighter. The equipment does not affect the gameplay in any way. Even the presence of a night vision device is not necessary, because you will turn it on anyway even without a special headdress. But the modifications to the weapons are beyond praise. You can customize your weapon to suit your style. If you love to actively attack bases - use a grenade launcher. Prefer to eliminate the enemy without any noise - a silencer and a telescopic sight will help you.
    [*] Partners. Yes, this game has a cooperative mode, but you shouldn't forget about artificial intelligence either. And in some cases, your artificial partners perform better assigned tasks than real players. Take for example the function [spoiler] "Synchronized shot" [/spoiler]. One press of a button and three opponents will instantly die. Your partners will never spoil a quiet operation and will always be able to "give first aid" to you.
    [*] Villains. Despite the large number of bosses that we need to get to, they are all different. Each fulfills its role and has a different character. Yes, this is an insignificant "Plus". However, when you watch (read) the intelligence data, you plunge even deeper into the universe of the game.
[/list]

[b] Disadvantages: [/b]
[list]
    [*] Pumping. The plot can be played without it. However, you will not experience all the delights of this game. Let's pretend you haven't improved anything. You will not be able to conduct more complex operations and you will not be able to call the rebels for help. And as for the number of resurrections, it generally decreases to a minimum. If you want to get absolutely all the functions, you will have to complete the tasks of the rebels. The only way they differ from each other is only in location. The tasks themselves are not boring, but the same type.
    [*]Artificial Intelligence. If the AI ​​of the partners is amazing, then the civilians suffer. They can run out under the sight or throw themselves under the wheels. To be honest, they will cause a lot of problems. Then during assignments they will interfere. Everything would be fine, but after three killed residents in a row, the mission will fail and you will have to start all over again.
    [*]Technics. It's not bad, but the physics is awful. But once you think that you are driving a toy car, not a real car. If ground transportation is even more or less, then air transportation is terrible. The physics is awful, you don't feel the same plane. However, there is one "plus": the control is very easy.
[/list]

[h1] Is Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon® Wildlands worth your attention? [/h1]
Game for an amateur. If you are not embarrassed by the constant execution of the same actions and are not afraid of difficulties due to gaming conventions - definitely take it. However, I advise you to purchase this product at a discount, which appear very often. And if you do not approve of such a gameplay, I do not recommend it.
This is not a one-time game! If you have already started playing, then I advise you to delve into the plot. Then you will understand the whole plot and the purpose of the game.

[h1] Conclusion. [/h1]
Will I keep playing? Yes! I really liked the game and I will continue to play it, starting to go through two expansions and completing the remaining achievements.
I really hope I helped someone.
[b] Have a nice day everyone! [/b]

Dude, okay, so this game seems really good, but there is one thing that absolutely ruins it.

It's the Watchman mission. I played for 8 hours, then made the mistake of entering the "La Cruz" province. All of a sudden, it starts this Watchman mission. You can't get out of it, you can't come back to it later, you must complete it now, even if you're underprepared - the game doesn't care. You're locked in. You must do it now, before anything else. It will game over and reload you if you try to do anything else.

It's apparently one of if not the most unreasonably difficult missions in the game. I tried to complete it like 20 times, on the literal easiest difficulty, then I was like, screw this, I'd rather delete my save game, start over, and avoid starting this mission at all until I feel adequately prepared.

The thing is, usually, you can fly around anywhere you want, and if you want intel on a region, you land, you get out of the vehicle, and you walk around for a second. After 8 hours of gameplay, I decided I would just go region-to-region and get all of the "major intel" locations. That's when I found myself locked into the Watchman mission, wasted several more hours banging my head against a wall trying to complete it, and decided to instead just start over.

Well, that thing about having to LAND in a region before you get intel? It turns out that doesn't apply to the Watchman mission. I started a new game, started flying from region to region to get the intel, then made the mistake of FLYING OVER this region, and boom. The Watchman mission came up and I was locked in again, killing my second new game.

This is so pathetically and terribly broken. There is no reason not to make this a mission you can do at your leisure, like every other mission in the game. There is no reason not to provide the player with a "quit mission" option in the start menu. There is no reason to make it so unreasonably difficult.

If you want to enjoy this game, do yourself a favor - do not under any circumstances ever even come CLOSE to the La Cruz region, unless you're ludicrously over-prepared or have some absolute GOATs in your co-op party. To be fair, I have only played single player, I guess I should call in some help to get past this absolute save killer. But there really is no excuse for it to be this way.

I'm starting a third new save file, I'm backing up my saves (autosave with no "former" saves you can reload is also a terrible design choice, especially with a mission like this in the game), I'm treating the La Cruz province like literal Hell and never entering it under any circumstances until I've beaten the game in its entirety, and F.U. to whoever thought this was a good idea.

This game can be both incredibly engaging, and incredibly infuriating. I have been playing at the highest difficulty, with no HUD, and that has required me to play very tactically, forcing me to engage with systems I would have otherwise left untouched. The semi-realistic ballistics (It doesn't appear to take wind into account), adds a subtle level of difficulty as it requires you to understand how your weapon will work in any given situation. I took the time to document the individual characteristics of my favored weapons, things such as bullet drop and travel time, which is something I couldn't say for any other game I've played. My playstyle has been centered around using sniper rifles, and making shots at long range (400+ meters) has proven to be very satisfying. The game is exceptional when playing with friends. Playing spotter for my friend as he infiltrates a base was some of the best gameplay I've experienced this year. The version of Bolivia in the game is beautiful and expansive, with a wide variety of environments, from salt flats to mountain jungles. This combined with the dynamic weather leads to picturesque, almost breathtaking views. There were moments in my playthrough where these vistas lined up with the games soundtrack in a rather sublime way.

 However, the game is not without it's flaws. The story is completely forgettable, serving as little more than an excuse to get to the next mission. The variety among the side missions leaves something to be desired. You will find yourself stealing the same planes and stopping the same convoys over and over again. The AI leaves something to be desired, and I have found myself yelling in frustration at multiple times playing the game. The 3 teammate NPC's are next to worthless outside of there use for sync shot. All to often I find myself being flanked and killed by enemies while my teammates did nothing to help. More often than not they will prioritize reviving you over killing enemies. This has led to situations where they are reviving me in front of the enemy who just took me down, who then proceeds to immediately open fire again, usually resulting in being knocked right back down again. They are constantly repeating the same boring dialog, and telling the same unfunny jokes over and over again. The rebel NPC's that are meant to act as your reinforcements have proven to be more of a hindrance than anything. I have had them show up and engage the enemy while I am trying to infiltrate a base, blowing my cover and getting me killed (cause as soon as the enemy are fighting the rebels, they know exactly where I am as well). The environments have a tendency to be finicky, with many surfaces seeming like they should  be climbable when they were not. There were multiple times where I found myself stuck in some mountain cliff, forcing me to abandon whatever I was doing and fast travel away.

Also, the cars don't have horns. Come on Ubi, it's 2017, put a horn on that car.

Overall, I've really enjoyed my time with Wildlands. I would recommend picking it up either if you have a friend you plan to play it with, or if you happen to see it on sale.
